And for {{ls}}ome other Confe{{ls}}sors not Bi{{ls}}hops.}}A certaine noble man vvent into a farre countrie to take to him {{ls}}elf a kingdom, and to returne. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=13}}† And calling his ten {{ls}}eruants, he gaue them ten poundes, and {{ls}}aid to them, Occupie til I come. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=14}}† And his citizens hated him: and they {{ls}}ent a legacie after him, {{ls}}aying, VVe vvil not haue this man reigne ouer vs. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=15}}† And it came to pa{{ls}}{{ls}}e after he returned, hauing receiued his kingdom: and he commaunded his {{ls}}eruants to be called, to vvhom he gaue the money: that he might knovv how much euery man had gained by occupying. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=16}}† And the fir{{ls}}t came, {{ls}}aying, Lord, thy pound hath gotten ten poundes. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=17}}† And he {{ls}}aid to him, VVel fare thee good {{ls}}eruant, becau{{ls}}e thou ha{{ls}}t been faithful in a litle, thou {{ls}}halt haue povver ouer {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ Marke here again{{ls}}t the aduer{{ls}}aries, that the rewards of the{{ls}}e two good {{ls}}eruants be diuers & vnaequal, according to the diuer{{ls}}itie or inequality of their gaines, that is, their merites. and yet one receiueth the peny ''(Mt. 20, 9''.) as wel as the other, that is, heauen or life euerla{{ls}}ting.}}∷ ten cities. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=18}}† And the {{ls}}econd came, {{ls}}aying, Lord, thy pound hath made fiue poundes. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=19}}† And he {{ls}}aid to him, And be thou ouer fiue cities. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=20}}† And an other came, {{ls}}aying, Lord, loe here thy pound, vvhich I haue had laid vp in a napkin. {{verse|chapter=19|verse=21}}† for I feared thee, becau{{ls}}e thou art an austêre man: thou take{{ls}}t vp that thou did{{ls}}t not {{ls}}et dovvne, and thou reape{{ls}}t<noinclude>{{rh||Bb|that}}</noinclude>
